findings.claim: The BCS table states that Class 2 drugs (low solubility, high permeability) do not require an in-vivo bioequivalence study.
findings.evidence: "Class 2 | Low | High | Drug is dissolution limited and well absorbed / Bioavailability is controlled by the dosage form and rate of release of the drug substance / Not require in-vivo bioequivalence study". The same table gives Class 3 (high solubility, low permeability) as "Require in-vivo bioequivalence study", which inverts the biowaiver rule.
findings.fix_hint: ICH M9 grants BCS-based biowaivers to Class 1 and Class 3 only, so Class 2 is the class the table gets backwards. State the ICH M9 rule first, then add, separately and with its conditions, the narrow Class 2 weak-acid pathway that the current Egyptian Drug Authority bioequivalence guideline allows - the brief names the EDA framework, so the national exception belongs in the text rather than being folded into the ICH rule.

findings.claim: "Highly permeable" is defined as extent of absorption >= 90% of the administered dose (F >= 0.9).
findings.evidence: "The extent of absorption in human >= 90% of the administered dose based on mass-balance (AUC) or in comparison to IV reference dose i.e. if F >= 0.9".
findings.fix_hint: The 90% figure is from the withdrawn 2000 FDA BCS guidance. ICH M9 (2019) uses >= 85%. Update the number and name the guidance.

findings.claim: "Highly soluble" is defined over a pH range of 1 to 7.5, referenced to the highest dose strength.
findings.evidence: "The highest dose strength is soluble in < 250 ml water over a pH range of 1 - 7.5 (pH range of GIT)".
findings.fix_hint: ICH M9 defines high solubility over pH 1.2 to 6.8 at 37 +/- 1 C, referenced to the highest single therapeutic dose rather than the highest strength. Correct both the range and the reference quantity.

findings.claim: The bioequivalence chapter never states the acceptance criterion that decides whether two products are bioequivalent.
findings.evidence: The section "Evaluation of the data" covers the analytical method, the pharmacokinetic parameters and ANOVA, and ends at "Significance level of 5% [0.05]". The 90% confidence interval of the test/reference geometric mean ratio for AUC and Cmax falling within 80.00-125.00% appears nowhere in the 109 pages.
findings.fix_hint: Add the criterion explicitly, per ICH M13A: log-transform AUC and Cmax, compute the 90% confidence interval of the test/comparator geometric mean ratio, and require 80.00-125.00%, with the narrowed interval for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs. This is the one thing a student must carry out of this chapter.

findings.claim: The text presents a 95% confidence level, applied as a test for a difference, as the statistical basis of a bioequivalence decision.
findings.evidence: "2) Confidence level of 95% is required means that confidence that the difference is significant is >= 95% 3) Significance level of 5% [0.05]".
findings.fix_hint: Bioequivalence uses a 90% confidence interval, which is the two one-sided tests procedure at alpha = 0.05 each. Correct the interval and the logic: the decision is equivalence within limits, not a significance test for a difference.

findings.claim: Oligopeptides are said to be degraded by lactase and maltase.
findings.evidence: "Oligopeptides are degraded by lactase [its deficiency cause lactose intolerance] and maltase peptidase enzymes (integral membrane proteins not a soluble lumen enzymes) into free amino acids and very small peptides".
findings.fix_hint: Lactase and maltase are brush-border disaccharidases; they hydrolyse carbohydrates, not peptides. Oligopeptides are hydrolysed by brush-border peptidases (aminopeptidase N, dipeptidyl peptidase IV) and cytosolic peptidases. Remove the lactose-intolerance aside, which belongs to carbohydrate digestion.

findings.claim: Tetracyclines are given as the example of quaternary nitrogen compounds.
findings.evidence: "a) Highly ionized or charged molecules over all pH range of GIT e.g. quaternary nitrogen compounds (tetracyclines) i.e. with extreme pKa (either too high or too low)".
findings.fix_hint: Tetracyclines are amphoteric, with three ionisable groups; they are not quaternary ammonium compounds. Use a genuine quaternary example and keep tetracycline as a separate ion-pair example on its own merits.

findings.claim: Metabolism differences are attributed to race: black men are said to be faster acetylators and metabolizers than white men.
findings.evidence: "4) Metabolism may vary due to intrinsic genetic factors (e.g. black men are faster acetylators and metabolizers than white men) and extrinsic factors". Confirmed in the source PDF text, page 50, so it is not a conversion artefact.
findings.fix_hint: Acetylation phenotype is set by NAT2 genotype, whose allele frequencies differ between populations but do not map onto skin colour, and the stated direction is not what the literature shows. Replace with the pharmacogenetic mechanism (NAT2 slow and fast acetylators, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 polymorphisms) and cite it.

findings.claim: The text asserts that Egyptians carry a genetic defect in the vitamin B12 absorption carrier.
findings.evidence: "Egyptians have a genetic defect for carrier of vitamin B12 absorption", placed inside the facilitated-diffusion column of the carrier-transport table. Confirmed in the source PDF text, page 63.
findings.fix_hint: No source supports a population-wide defect; hereditary intrinsic-factor and cubilin defects are rare in every population. Remove the claim, and move B12 out of the facilitated-diffusion column: its uptake is intrinsic-factor-mediated receptor endocytosis.

findings.claim: The flow-through cell flow rate is given as two incompatible ranges in the same sentence.
findings.evidence: "Flow rate ranges from 4 to 16 mL/min (usually maintained between 10 and 100 mL/min)". Confirmed in the source PDF text, page 104.
findings.fix_hint: USP <711> Apparatus 4 uses 4, 8 and 16 mL/min as the standard rates. Delete the second range or attribute it to a named non-compendial use.

findings.claim: Therapeutic index is used to mean the concentration band between MEC and MTC.
findings.evidence: "2. Allow maintaining drug concentration within therapeutic range (TI) thus optimize the therapy" at line 164 equates the therapeutic range with TI. The same equation is made in the plasma-curve diagram on page 5 of the source PDF, whose labels read "MEC / MTC / Therapeutic index (TI)"; that diagram is one of 14 images on that page and so has no text in ingest/normalized.md.
findings.fix_hint: The band between MEC and MTC is the therapeutic range or therapeutic window. Therapeutic index is a ratio (TD50/ED50, or MTC/MEC when defined on concentrations). Separate the two terms in the text and in the redrawn figure.

findings.claim: Bioequivalence volunteer eligibility is given as weight 54-91 kg and age 20-50 years, with no source.
findings.evidence: "Weight of volunteers 54 - 91 kg (affect Vd), age 20 - 50 years" and, in the single-dose protocol, "Weight: 54 - 91 kg.".
findings.fix_hint: ICH M13A specifies age at least 18 years and BMI typically within 18.5-30 kg/m2, not an absolute weight band. Update and cite, or label the figures explicitly as the historical FDA criterion.

findings.claim: The Noyes-Whitney equation exists only as an embedded picture, so the only searchable, readable form of it in the book is its symbol list.
findings.evidence: Page 102 of the source PDF carries exactly one embedded image, positioned between "The overall rate of drug dissolution may be described by the Noyes-Whitney equation" and "Where dC/dt is the rate of drug dissolution at time t". No character of the equation appears in the page's text layer.
findings.fix_hint: Set dC/dt = (D x A / h)(Cs - C) as real, numbered text before the symbol list, and add the sink-condition simplification (C much smaller than Cs) that the later particle-size discussion depends on.

findings.claim: The Wagner-Nelson worked example tabulates plasma concentrations in mg/ml.
findings.evidence: The table header reads "Cp (mg/ml)" with values from 0.6 to 6 following a 100 mg oral dose; 6 mg/ml would be 6 g/L of drug in plasma, and the whole 100 mg dose dissolved in one litre could not reach it.
findings.fix_hint: The values are microgram/ml. Correct the header and carry the unit through every derived column (AUC in microgram.hr/ml) so the Ab/Ab-infinity ratio is dimensionless by construction.

findings.claim: Example 16 is under-specified: the recovered amounts do not account for the whole dose, and the text does not say whether the remainder is lost or simply unmeasured.
findings.evidence: "A single dose (100 mg) of a drug is given orally, the drug is systemically available, total amount of unchanged drug recovered in urine is 60 mg & total amount of metabolite recovered in urine is 30 mg". Solving for fu needs a stated assumption about the missing 10 mg, and the question asks for Clr and Clnr, which depend on it.
findings.fix_hint: State the assumption the answer uses - either that recovery is complete and the numbers should read 70/30, or that the remaining 10 mg leaves by an unmeasured non-renal route - so that fu is determined rather than guessed.

findings.claim: Mathematics is carried in two forms that both defeat reading, search and reuse: embedded pictures, and Symbol-font characters in floating text boxes with subscripts set as separate runs.
findings.evidence: The source PDF embeds 354 images across 61 of its 109 pages, and its font list includes /Symbol alongside the text faces. The consequence is visible wherever the text layer is read: the two-compartment model comes out as "| K | 12 | Central (1) | Tissue (2) | K | 21" and the first-order decay law as "logD B =logD B - Kt / 2.303" spread across seven cells, with the minus and equals signs surviving only as the glyph pair for Symbol code points.
findings.fix_hint: Set every equation as real text with real subscripts, number them, and keep one symbol table. The printed page is legible today, but nothing else is: the book cannot be searched, read aloud, translated, reflowed or - as this project has just demonstrated - converted.

findings.claim: None of the 23 numbered examples is worked through: the "Answer" heading is followed by blank space or, in one case, by empty tables.
findings.evidence: Examples 1 to 23 appear at lines 434 to 2152. Example 1 is followed by "Answer" and then the page break at line 441; Example 8 (line 621) is followed by "Answer", the headings "(1) Urinary Excretion Method" and "(2) Sigma - Minus Method", and two tables whose calculation columns are empty (lines 641-667). The only fully worked examples are the two unnumbered ones, at line 2276 (non-compartmental analysis, with its AUC/AUMC table) and line 4431 (comparing three formulations, answered in prose).
findings.fix_hint: Work all 23 through in print: the equation chosen, the substitution with units, the arithmetic and the answer with its unit. The two unnumbered examples show the standard to match. This is the whole reason a student opens a calculation-based course book.

findings.claim: Example numbering runs out of order: 22 and 23 appear in the oral-absorption section before 19, 20 and 21 in the multiple-dosing section.
findings.evidence: Example 22 is at line 1559 and Example 23 at line 1700, both inside "Pharmacokinetics of drug absorption"; Examples 19 (line 2130), 20 (line 2138) and 21 (line 2146) follow in "Multiple dosage regimens".
findings.fix_hint: Renumber examples per chapter (Example 7.1, 7.2, ...) so insertion or removal never breaks the sequence again.

findings.claim: The method of residuals is the central technique of two chapters and is never demonstrated on numbers.
findings.evidence: It is described twice - for two-compartment IV data (lines 752-784) and for oral absorption (lines 1500-1558) - each time as prose plus an uncaptioned sketch. Example 10 (line 859) and Example 22 (line 1559) supply data for it, and neither is worked.
findings.fix_hint: Work one dataset end to end with the residual table visible: the extrapolated terminal line, the back-extrapolated values, the residuals, the residual-line slope, and Ka or alpha read from it.

findings.claim: The book states no learning objectives, at any level.
findings.evidence: The word "objective" occurs twice in the whole 109-page source text, and neither is a learning objective: "used for the same therapeutic or clinical objective" (therapeutic alternatives) and "The objective is that no significant dissolution occurs in the acid phase" (enteric-coated testing). There is no outcome list and no "by the end of this topic" statement anywhere.
findings.fix_hint: Give each chapter 3-5 measurable objectives written with verbs the assessment can test (calculate, derive, distinguish, select), and tag every question and worked example to one of them.

findings.claim: The document has no chapter structure: nothing is numbered as a chapter, and no section carries an introduction or a summary.
findings.evidence: The word "chapter" occurs zero times in the 109-page source text and "summar" zero times. Section titles such as "Clearance" (line 418), "Intravenous Infusion" (line 871) and "NON-LINEAR PHARMACOKINETICS" (line 2430) carry no number and no consistent capitalisation, and the contents page (lines 70-85) lists subjects rather than chapters.
findings.fix_hint: Impose the 14 contents-page subjects as 14 numbered chapters with a fixed internal shape: objectives, concept, key equations, worked examples, takeaways, questions.

findings.claim: No figure in the book has a number, a caption or a cross-reference from the text.
findings.evidence: The source PDF embeds 354 images across 61 of its 109 pages, and the word "Figure" occurs zero times in its text layer. A caption or a cross-reference would be text and would appear; none does. The images therefore stand unlabelled wherever they fall on the page.
findings.fix_hint: Redraw each diagram as a numbered figure with axis labels, units and a caption stating what the reader should take from it, and reference each one from the paragraph that needs it.

findings.claim: The contents page lists 14 subjects with page numbers, but no heading in the body matches those entries, so the list cannot be used to navigate.
findings.evidence: The contents lists "Two compartment, IV bolus, plasma data 16"; the body at that point reads "Two compartment open model following I V route (single dose)" (line 669) as ordinary text.
findings.fix_hint: Make the contents a generated table of contents over real headings, so entry, heading and page can never drift apart.

findings.claim: Clearance is introduced twice with near-identical wording, once inside the IV-bolus material and once as its own subject.
findings.evidence: Lines 418-422 and lines 1146-1150 both open "The volume of the fluid (plasma or blood) containing the drug which is cleared of the drug per unit time, so if clearance of penicillin is 15 ml / min in a patient with Vd = 12 liters...", and the Cl = K x Vd relation is derived twice (lines 426-433 and 1156-1161).
findings.fix_hint: Keep the full treatment in the clearance chapter and leave a one-line forward reference at the first mention.

findings.claim: Untranslated Arabic lecture glosses are left inside the English text.
findings.evidence: Four occurrences, quoted as they stand in ingest/normalized.md (the PDF stores them with reversed glyph order, so they read backwards): "luminal membrane of absorbing epithelia is studded ببحم with microvilli" (line 2894); "Generic Name: The nonproprietary name دحاو ىأ كلم شم" (line 4014, for "mish milk ay wahid", not owned by anyone); "Criteria for waiver ءافعإ of in vivo bioavailability study" (line 4675, i'faa, exemption); "human cadaver ةثج skin" (line 4971, juththa, corpse).
findings.fix_hint: These are lecture asides. Remove them from the body; where the gloss is genuinely useful, move the term into a bilingual glossary entry.

findings.claim: A point is emphasised with a run of about seventy exclamation marks.
findings.evidence: "kinetics of the drug in some subjects is best described by 2-compartment model while in other subjects it is best described by 3-compartment model!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!". The same habit appears at lines 1328 and 4638 ("?!").
findings.fix_hint: Replace with a sentence that says why the observation matters: the compartment count is a property of the data and the sampling design, not of the drug.

findings.claim: The book carries about a hundred symbols and defined terms, has no glossary or symbol table, and reuses one symbol for two quantities.
findings.evidence: Symbols are defined inline where first used (Cp, Cp0, K, Ke, Knr, Km, Ka, Vd, Vp, Vt, A, B, alpha, beta, K12, K21, AUC, AUMC, MRT, MAT, MTT, Du, ARE, R, tau, f, fu, F, Q). Km is the hepatic elimination rate constant at line 1191 and the Michaelis constant at line 2459.
findings.fix_hint: Add a symbol table in the front matter and a glossary at the back, and rename one of the two Km uses.

findings.claim: The only assessment is the 23 unanswered examples: there is no question set, no answer key, no rationale and no link from any item to a stated outcome.
findings.evidence: Beyond the numbered examples (F-018), the book poses two rhetorical questions in the body - "To study removal of a drug from the body, would you use t1/2 or ClT? Why?" (line 1328, answered immediately at line 1334) and "Reduction in particle size is not always helpful, rationalize?" (line 3724). There is no end-of-topic question set, no multiple-choice item and no rationale anywhere in the 109 pages.
findings.fix_hint: Add per-chapter questions with answers and rationales, mixed between recall, calculation and interpretation, each tagged to an objective. The two rhetorical questions already in the text are good models for the interpretation items.

findings.claim: A 109-page course book cites three textbooks in total and carries no in-text citation anywhere.
findings.evidence: The References page lists Aulton (6th ed., 2021), Ansel (12th ed., 2021) and Shargel & Yu (8th ed., 2022). No numbered marker, author-year reference or footnote appears in the body.
findings.fix_hint: Add in-text citations for every number, criterion and named study, and keep the consolidated list at the back as the user chose.

findings.claim: Named studies, dates and regulatory statements are asserted with no source the reader can check, and one date is wrong by a decade.
findings.evidence: "reported by DeHann and co-workers (1972)" (line 2138), "Regamey and associates (1973)" (line 2146), "Concept of bioavailability was introduced in 1945 by Oser et al" (line 3987), "In 1961 FDA said that bioavailability is the same as biological availability" (line 4001), "The Australian outbreak of phenytoin intoxication" (line 3921), "by Amidon et al in 1985" (line 4689). None appears in the reference list, and the Amidon BCS paper is 1995.
findings.fix_hint: Trace each one to its primary source and cite it; correct the Amidon date to 1995.

findings.claim: The regulatory chapters describe a framework that predates the guidance now in force.
findings.evidence: The bioequivalence and BCS material uses the FDA-only vocabulary of the 1990s (Orange Book, RLD, Latin-square crossover, 54-91 kg volunteers, 90% permeability threshold, pH 1-7.5) and nowhere mentions ICH M9 (2019) on biowaivers or ICH M13A (2024) on bioequivalence study design, which are the harmonised texts the Egyptian Drug Authority and the EMA both apply.
findings.fix_hint: Reframe the chapter around ICH M9 and ICH M13A, keeping the historical FDA material only where it is still the operative rule, and add the Egyptian Drug Authority guideline as the national layer.

findings.claim: Volume of distribution is said to change only in pathological conditions.
findings.evidence: "Vd is a proportionality constant for each drug (under normal healthy condition) but change only in pathological conditions e.g. renal dysfunction, liver cirrhosis, CHF and edematous conditions".
findings.fix_hint: Vd also varies with age, body composition, pregnancy and plasma protein binding in healthy people. Soften to "changes most markedly in" and add the physiological sources of variation.

findings.claim: The washout period between study periods is given as 10 half-lives with no source.
findings.evidence: "Period means the time interval in which a study is performed (2 period study means it is performed in 2 different days separated by washout period of 10 t1/2)".
findings.fix_hint: Ten half-lives is conservative rather than wrong, so this is a citation gap and not a content error. ICH M13A asks for a washout long enough that pre-dose concentrations are negligible, commonly at least five terminal half-lives; state that minimum, cite M13A, and keep ten as the safe practical choice.

findings.claim: The accumulation half-life formula is stated without its derivation or its domain of validity.
findings.evidence: "Accumulation t1/2 = t1/2 [1 + 3.3 log (Ka / (Ka - K))]" is given, then reduced for IV by asserting "Ka approaches infinity and K is very small compared to Ka thus K can be removed from the equation", which leaves log(1) = 0 unstated as the reason the bracket collapses to 1.
findings.fix_hint: Show the collapse explicitly: as Ka/(Ka - K) tends to 1, its logarithm tends to 0, so accumulation t1/2 equals elimination t1/2. State that the formula assumes first-order absorption with Ka greater than K.

findings.claim: Absolute bioavailability of 1 is equated with complete gastrointestinal absorption.
findings.evidence: "A.B = F (fraction of dose that is bioavailable) 1) For I.V route (vascular route) = 1 2) For oral route (extravascular route) F = 0 - 1 (0 for completely unavailable drugs and 1 for completely absorbed drugs)".
findings.fix_hint: A completely absorbed drug can still have F well below 1 through gut-wall and hepatic first-pass metabolism, which the book itself covers two pages earlier. Separate fraction absorbed (fa) from intestinal availability (Fg), hepatic availability (Fh) and systemic bioavailability F = fa x Fg x Fh, and use propranolol, already cited in the text, as the worked case.

findings.claim: Release mechanism is listed among the attributes on which pharmaceutical equivalents may differ.
findings.evidence: The two-column table "Pharmaceutic equivalents: drug products contain / The same [1) Dosage form 2) Active ingredient 3) Conc. or strength 4) Route of administration] / But may differ in [1) Shape 2) Scoring configuration 3) Release mechanism 4) Packaging 5) Excipients 6) expiration date 7) Within certain limits labeling]".
findings.fix_hint: Products with different release mechanisms are different dosage forms, so they are pharmaceutical alternatives, not equivalents; an immediate-release and an extended-release tablet of the same drug are the standard counter-example. Move release mechanism into the "same" column and check the pharmaceutical-alternatives definition that follows for the same confusion.

findings.claim: A comparator-selection rule is stated that does not exist: the reference standard "should contain the drug at least 5% of the whole product".
findings.evidence: In the list of reference-standard requirements: "- Usually it is Innovator's product ... - Should contain the drug at least 5% of the whole product".
findings.fix_hint: No guidance sets a minimum API fraction for a comparator. The 5% is most likely a garbled memory of the permitted difference in measured content between test and comparator batches. Replace with the actual ICH M13A comparator-selection and batch-potency requirements.

findings.claim: Four pharmacologically active metabolites are listed as examples of toxic metabolites.
findings.evidence: "2) Metabolite can be toxic e.g. Fluoxetine to norfluoxetine, propranolol to 4-OH propranolol, verapamil to norverapamil, diazepam to desmethyldiazepam and toxic metabolites of acetaminophen". Norfluoxetine, 4-hydroxypropranolol, norverapamil and desmethyldiazepam are active metabolites; only the acetaminophen example (NAPQI) is a toxic metabolite. The preceding item in the same list already covers active metabolites.
findings.fix_hint: Keep NAPQI and add genuine reactive or toxic metabolites (for example normeperidine, or acyl glucuronides); move the other four into the active-metabolite item above, where the same list already sits.

findings.claim: A dosage-form ranking of bioavailability is asserted as a general fact rather than a heuristic.
findings.evidence: "The bioavailability of a drug from the various dosage forms is of the following order: Solution > emulsion > suspension > soft gelatin capsule > hard gelatin capsule > tablets. Among tablets, the order is: uncoated tablets > Coated tablets > Enteric coated > SR/CR products", with no qualifier. A shorter version of the same ranking appears at line 3768.
findings.fix_hint: Kept as minor rather than major: the ranking is standard teaching in the textbooks the book cites, and the defect is the missing qualifier, not the ordering. Introduce it as a general tendency, say that it follows from the number of steps before absorption, and give one counter-example where formulation overturns it.
